lesson_title: Balloons and Tug-of-War: Molecular Shapes and Polarity
hook_text: Knot four balloons together and they snap into the exact shape of methane. Molecules play by balloon rules.
clip_script: Knot four balloons together at their necks and let go. They refuse to lie flat — they snap into a tripod with one balloon standing up. A tetrahedron. Here's the mad part: that is EXACTLY the shape of methane, and for exactly the same reason. Electron pairs around an atom all carry negative charge, so they shove each other as far apart as space allows — balloons in miniature. Two pairs? A dead-straight line, like carbon dioxide. Four pairs? The tripod, 109,5 degrees. But watch out — some balloons are invisible. Lone pairs shove like all the rest, yet no atom sits at their corner. Ammonia hides one balloon and shows you a pyramid. Water hides two and shows you a bend — three atoms at an angle. And that little bend rearranges the planet. Every bond is a tug-of-war for electrons: oxygen out-pulls hydrogen, so each of water's bonds has a charged negative end and a charged positive end. In straight carbon dioxide the two pulls face off and cancel perfectly. In BENT water they can't — the whole molecule keeps a charged side. That is why water dissolves salt, grips glass, and boils hot enough for tea. Geometry, quietly running chemistry.
visual_style: Real party balloons snapping into a tetrahedron, morphing into glowing electron clouds around an atom; lone pairs rendered as ghost balloons fading out; tug-of-war ropes stretched across bonds, closing on a bent water molecule glowing red and blue at its charged ends.
mood: Hands-on and surprising — party balloons casually explaining the universe.
pacing: Physical playful open, crisp shape-by-shape middle, resonant close on the bend that runs the world.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never draw a wrong molecular shape again.
